item.title: Subsidised fertiliser being smuggled into Myanmar
item.description:
Aman paddy has been cultivated on nearly 500 acres of land in Uttar Pukuria village of Rajapalong Union in Ukhiya, Cox’s Bazar. More than a hundred farmers in the village have complained that they are unable to obtain urea fertiliser, which they need after transplanting the rice seedlings.

Mohammad Tayyub, 45, a resident of the village, is one of these farmers. He said he went to a dealer in Ukhiya Bazar on 30 September to buy 30kg of fertiliser. After waiting in line for nearly seven hours, he received only 5kg. He is worried about how he will protect the crops on his seven kani of land (one kani equals 40 decimals) with this amount of fertiliser.

Like Tayyub, other farmers in the village are also worried about the fertiliser shortage. It has been learned after speaking to farmers that the shortage is not limited to Ukhiya; most areas of Cox’s Bazar, including Teknaf, Ramu, Eidgaon, Pekua and Chakaria, are also facing a fertiliser crisis. The crisis is worsening day by day as several syndicates smuggle fertiliser into Myanmar.

Smuggling into Myanmar

Speaking to officials of the Department of Agricultural Extension and fertiliser dealers, it was learnt that the government provides substantial subsidies on fertiliser sales to ensure that farmers receive fertiliser at affordable prices. Currently, the government-fixed price of a 50kg sack of urea fertiliser at the open market or dealer level is Tk 1,350 (Tk 27 per kg).

However, a sack of fertiliser sells for more than Tk 8,000 in Myanmar’s Rakhine State. As a result, several syndicates are smuggling fertiliser allocated to farmers into Myanmar in pursuit of higher profits. In exchange, consignments of drugs are brought into the country.

A research report recently published by the World Bank stated that nearly 80 per cent of the Agriculture Ministry's budget is spent on fertiliser subsidies. These subsidies have helped maintain agricultural production and price stability.

Speaking to traders involved in imports and exports through Teknaf Land Port, it was learnt that urea fertiliser and fuel oil are being smuggled from Bangladesh into Rakhine State by taking advantage of geographical proximity and the unstable internal situation in Myanmar. Smuggling syndicates involved in the trade bring yaba and crystal meth from Myanmar in exchange for fertiliser and fuel oil.

There is no urea fertiliser manufacturing plant in Rakhine State. Moreover, the unstable situation has disrupted the supply of fertiliser to the state, prompting local farmers to buy fertiliser smuggled from Bangladesh at higher prices.

According to information from the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) and the Coast Guard, between 1 June and 20 September this year, the BGB and Coast Guard seized 247,908kg of urea fertiliser in separate drives along the Teknaf, Ukhiya and Naikhongchhari borders and the Naf River. During this period, 127 people involved in smuggling were arrested.

Most recently, on 2 October, the BGB seized 81 sacks of urea fertiliser and smuggled goods worth Tk 700,000 during a drive along the Ghumdhum border in Naikhongchhari.

Lieutenant Colonel Md Foyezul Kabir, commanding officer of the Naikhongchhari 11 BGB, said surveillance along the border had been strengthened to prevent smuggling of fertiliser, fuel oil and other goods.

Locals said fertiliser and fuel oil were being smuggled through at least 23 border points, including Anjumanpara and Balukhali in Palongkhali, Ukhiya; Whykong, Kanjarpara and Ulubunia in Teknaf; Leda and Damdamiya in Hnila; and Ghumdhum in Naikhongchhari. In most cases, the people assisting in the smuggling are arrested, but the masterminds remain beyond the reach of law enforcement agencies.

Coast Guard media officer Lieutenant Commander Sabbir Alam said more than 70 smugglers had already been arrested, along with fertiliser-laden trawlers, during Coast Guard operations while they were attempting to smuggle fertiliser into Myanmar through coastal waters. Efforts were underway to bring the masterminds to justice as well.

M Gafur Uddin Chowdhury, chairman of Palongkhali Union Parishad in Ukhiya, said those involved in smuggling fertiliser and fuel were also bringing in consignments of yaba, ice and other drugs. There are no legitimate transactions in dollars or taka on the other side of the border (Myanmar), he added.

Shahjahan Chowdhury, a member of parliament from Cox’s Bazar-4 (Ukhiya-Teknaf) constituency, said several syndicates were involved in fertiliser smuggling. Although law enforcement agencies had seized large quantities of fertiliser and major consignments of yaba and arrested smugglers during raids, the masterminds remained beyond their reach. They must be identified and brought to justice, he said.

Farmers in distress

Gias Uddin, a farmer from Whykong Union in Teknaf, said, “I am going from one dealer to another in search of fertiliser, but I am not getting the amount I need. Yet fertiliser is being smuggled across the border almost every day.”

Abdul Gafur, a farmer from Kochubunia in Teknaf Sadar Union, said those with smaller plots of land somehow manage to get fertiliser, but farmers with larger plots are unable to obtain the amount they need. Dealers are selling fertiliser to many people who are not farmers. Later, these fertiliser stocks are handed over to smuggling syndicates.

Nawab Mia, a farmer from the Kachhapia area of Ramu, said he cultivated paddy on seven kani of land, but dealers turned him away, saying there was ‘no fertiliser available’. Left with no choice, he bought a small quantity of fertiliser from the market at double the price and spread it across his fields. Due to the continued shortage, Aman seedlings on one and a half kani of his land have turned yellow and are at risk of being destroyed.

Mohammad Kabir, president of the Ukhiya Upazila Fertiliser Dealers Association, said some unscrupulous traders were smuggling fertiliser allocated to farmers into Myanmar to make extra profits. As a result, fertiliser was not available in Ukhiya according to demand.

Regarding fertiliser smuggling, Bimal Kumar Pramanik, deputy director of the Department of Agricultural Extension, said several teams were monitoring markets to prevent smuggling. Special attention was being given to fertiliser sales in Teknaf and Ukhiya upazilas.

Dealers were submitting information on fertiliser sales to the Department of Agricultural Extension online after completing sales. Even so, action would be taken against the dealers concerned if allegations of illegal fertiliser sales were found to be true, he added.

item.title: 45th BCS: Recommended but dropped, allegations of state injustice; state minister assures re-verification
item.description:
Aleya Khanam is a self-respecting and hardworking woman from West Bejgram village in Hatibandha upazila of Lalmonirhat. Through her hard-earned income, she has raised her three children to be educated and responsible citizens. Her eldest daughter has completed her studies and settled down, while her youngest daughter has just started college. Her son, Shamim Al Mahadi, completed his studies at Bangladesh Agricultural University and was preparing for the Bangladesh Civil Service (BCS) examination.

Alongside farming, Aleya Khanam built her own cattle farm at home in an effort to become financially self-reliant. A year ago, when she received the news that her son had been finally recommended for appointment through the 45th BCS examination, she felt proud of him. She thought his merit had received its due recognition.

But that relief did not last long. Eleven long months passed waiting for the gazette notification. Finally, on the night of 14 October, the Ministry of Public Administration published the final gazette notification for the 45th BCS. Of the 1,807 candidates recommended by the Public Service Commission (PSC), 1,702 secured jobs, while 105 were left out. Shamim Al Mahadi, Aleya Begum's son, was among those unfairly excluded from the list.

The self-reliant woman was shocked and heartbroken when she did not find her son's name in the gazette. Speaking to this correspondent over the phone, Aleya Begum raised several questions that she considered reasonable.

She said, “Let anyone from the government come and investigate our area in person. If even one person in the village can say anything bad about my son, I will have no further claim to his job. They can also enquire about him from his school, college and university teachers. If he is found innocent everywhere, why should my son be deprived despite committing no wrongdoing?”

This mother does not understand the state's complex laws or administrative calculations. But she wants the truth to come out and does not want anyone to unfairly take away a right earned through merit.

Protests by candidates excluded from the gazette, threats of ‘suicide’

Stories like that of Mahadi, Aleya Begum's son, are shared by many meritorious candidates across the country. According to the candidates, despite successfully passing every stage of the PSC examination and receiving recommendations, their names were not included in the gazette without any specific reason. None of them has been accused of any criminal offence or crime against the state.

Having lost jobs they earned through merit and a transparent process, these young people have taken to the streets, facing extreme uncertainty about their future. They are holding a sit-in programme in front of the Raju Memorial Sculpture at Dhaka University in the capital.

The candidates who say they have been deprived have issued an extreme ultimatum, threatening to ‘kill themselves’ at Shahbagh unless a supplementary gazette is published immediately to ensure their appointments.

Speaking in a tearful voice during the sit-in programme, Nur-e-Alam, one of the candidates excluded from the gazette, said, “I was recommended for the Ansar cadre in the 44th BCS and am currently working as an assistant director.

But although I was newly recommended for the police cadre in the 45th BCS, my name has now been excluded from the gazette. I received clearance for my previous job, so I want the government to explain how I was excluded this time.”

Another candidate, Moniruzzaman, was recommended for the fisheries cadre. He said, “I worked relentlessly for four to five years and passed the BCS examination. Why should I face this punishment despite committing no crime? I do not know what answer to give my parents. We are not asking anyone for mercy; we want back the job we earned through our own merit.”

The candidates have placed five demands before the government. These include announcing a specific date for issuing a revised gazette, publishing a supplementary gazette for candidates who face no legal barriers, informing candidates in writing of the reasons for their exclusion, providing them with an opportunity to defend themselves, and ensuring transparency regarding the information used to exclude candidates during administrative verification.

What is police verification, and when did it begin?

After the final results of the BCS examination are announced, candidates undergo background verification before the gazette notification is published. The practice was introduced during the 1920s under British rule. At the time, its primary purpose was to suppress anti-British movements across the Indian subcontinent and examine candidates' political beliefs and whether they were involved in any activities against the then government before recruiting them to government jobs.

According to police guidelines, the verification process is supposed to establish only whether a candidate has any specific criminal case or record of criminal activity against them. However, allegations have persisted for a long time that this century-old practice from the British colonial era is being used to block merit-based appointments on the grounds of candidates' relatives' political identities or other irrelevant information.

Experts have also expressed frustration over the longstanding bureaucratic complications surrounding the BCS, irregularities in the name of verification and political discrimination.

‘State injustice must stop immediately’

Professor Rezwana Karim Snigdha of the Department of Anthropology at Jahangirnagar University told Prothom Alo, “In an independent state, holding back the merit and future of young people through an outdated verification system inherited from the British era is a major systemic flaw. If there is no specific information about a criminal offence against a candidate or a court conviction, depriving them of an opportunity on political or other pretexts is in no way acceptable. What, then, have we learned from such a historic mass uprising in 2024?

“I would say that the old practice of political party-based discrimination has now turned into ‘discrimination based on beliefs’. When the government runs the state, it cannot afford to harbour prejudice against any particular party, group or community. Doing so amounts to a breach of its oath. Depriving candidates who have demonstrated their merit of their rightful government jobs is a form of ‘state-structural corruption’. This state injustice must stop immediately,” she added.

State minister for public administration assures re-verification

Regarding the overall situation, State Minister for Public Administration Md Abdul Bari told Prothom Alo, “Verification is a regular part of the government recruitment process. It has always been there. It is nothing new. More than half of the candidates whose names did not appear in the gazette were temporarily excluded because of shortcomings in their required documents and other legal papers. The cases of the remaining candidates whose names were not included have come to our attention. The prime minister has given clear instructions that no citizen of the country should be deprived of their rightful entitlements under the state's laws and regulations."

“Therefore, an initiative will be taken to re-examine (re-verify) all the information concerning the candidates who were excluded. Everyone who is considered eligible for the job within the legal framework will be appointed. You have already seen in the 49th BCS that even after the publication of the final gazette, eligible candidates secured jobs through re-verification,” he added.

item.title: Japan to invest Tk 774.7 billion in Bangladesh
item.description:
Japan will invest one trillion yen, or USD 6.35 billion, in Bangladesh’s private sector over the next five years. The amount is equivalent to Tk 774.7 billion, calculated at an exchange rate of Tk 122 to the dollar.

Japan’s Nikkei Asia reported the development on Thursday. Reuters also published a report citing the Nikkei Asia article.

According to the report, the Japanese government has agreed to arrange the funds for investment in Bangladesh’s private sector. The investment is expected to be announced in a joint statement following a summit meeting between Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.

PM’s Japan visit: Reducing metro rail costs, loan interest rates likely to be discussed

Nikkei Asia reported that the announcement primarily aims to strengthen economic cooperation with Bangladesh and reduce China’s influence in Asia. Another objective is to establish Bangladesh as an investment hub.

The Japanese investment will be used in the automobile industry, other manufacturing sectors, and infrastructure development in the power and energy sectors. Japanese companies will also invest in the Bangladesh Special Economic Zone, developed through initiatives involving Japanese trading house Sumitomo Corporation and other partners.

Japan signed an economic partnership agreement with Bangladesh in February.

Ambassador to stay away from Tokyo during PM's Japan visit, ministry secretary sent to coordinate

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will visit Japan on 26 October for a four-day trip. On the second day of the visit, 27 October, he will hold bilateral talks with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi at her office. He will also attend a dinner hosted in his honour by the Japanese prime minister.

Foreign Secretary Asad Alam Siam said the visit would include discussions on expanding access for Bangladeshi products to the Japanese market, increasing Japanese investment and strengthening business ties.

At a press briefing at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Tuesday, he said discussions were under way on around eight memorandums of understanding (MoU) with Japan covering cooperation in agriculture, fisheries, human resource development and skills training, civil aviation and other sectors.

Several MoUs likely to be announced during PM's visit to Japan

Officials hope to sign three or four of the memorandums, he added.

The foreign secretary also expressed hope that the visit would create opportunities to expand cooperation in emerging areas, including renewable energy, the environment, science, technology, digital innovation, research and human resource development.

Japan is one of Bangladesh’s major development partners. It has supported the construction and implementation of several important infrastructure and connectivity projects, including the metro rail system, the third terminal at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport and the Matarbari deep-sea port.

item.title: Rivers swallow evidence, leaving murders unsolved Evidence of crime drifts with the current
item.description:
On 23 August, river police recovered the bodies of a woman, a child, a young man and a young woman from the Buriganga in Dhaka within a span of six hours. Black cloth was wrapped around the woman’s neck, while the child’s body was wrapped in a scarf.

The young man and woman had their hands tied together, and both had visible injuries. Police suspect they were murdered and their bodies dumped in the river to conceal the crimes. As their identities could not be established, all four bodies were buried as unidentified persons 11 days later.

Earlier, on 30 April last year, police recovered the body of an unidentified woman from a river in Narayanganj. A scarf had been wrapped around a bamboo pole beside the body. The woman was naked. She was buried as an unidentified person in the area. Her relatives later identified her after seeing photographs kept at the police station. The investigation revealed that she had been murdered. One person arrested in connection with the case subsequently gave a confessional statement in court.

River police recovered 2,064 bodies from rivers across Bangladesh between January 2021 and December 2025, a period of five years. Another 430 bodies were recovered between January and September this year. In total, 2,494 bodies were recovered over five years and nine months.

The bodies included victims of murder, people who accidentally fell into rivers and drowned, and people who died by suicide after jumping into the water.

River police officials say criminals dump bodies in rivers after committing murders to destroy evidence and evade arrest. They consider rivers a “safe place” to dispose of bodies and conceal their crimes.

The overall picture over five years and nine months

According to statistics from the River Police Headquarters, more men than women were among the bodies recovered between January 2021 and September this year. The remains of women and children were also found.

During this period, 392 murder cases were filed at police stations across the country, along with 26 cases involving suicide by jumping into rivers. Other deaths occurred while people were fishing, travelling or bathing, as well as in natural disasters and boat accidents. A total of 2,077 cases of unnatural death were filed.

According to figures provided by the River Police Headquarters, 1,739 of the recovered bodies were identified, while the identities of 755 remain unknown.

Cases are filed at the relevant police stations based on evidence found on recovered bodies. Bodies whose identities cannot be established are buried as unidentified persons by Anjuman Mufidul Islam, a charitable organisation.

DNA samples are collected from all recovered bodies, and photographs are taken and kept at the relevant police stations. If someone subsequently visits a police station and identifies a body after its burial, the police take steps to advance the case and further investigation based on the identification and other findings.

2021–25: 2,064 bodies recovered in five years

According to River Police Headquarters data, 318 bodies were recovered in 2021, 360 in 2022, 405 in 2023, 440 in 2024 and 541 in 2025. This brought the total to 2,064 over the five years. Murder cases were filed in 335 incidents in which the deaths were identified as homicides.

The number of bodies recovered increased every year during this period, reaching its highest level in 2025.

First nine months of this year: 430 bodies recovered

Of the 430 bodies recovered between January and September this year, 314 people were identified. The remaining 116 were buried as unidentified persons by Anjuman Mufidul Islam.

During these nine months, 57 murder cases were filed in connection with recovered bodies.

The police data also recorded 116 deaths while bathing, 57 while travelling or visiting places, 38 in boat accidents, 37 while fishing, 19 after falling from watercraft, two in natural disasters and one after jumping into a river. These categories accounted for 270 deaths.

The cause of death of another 104 people could not be determined, according to police data. Cases of unnatural death were filed in these instances.

Regional breakdown

River police have divided the country's waterways into 11 regions: Dhaka, Narayanganj, Chattogram, Chandpur, Barishal, Faridpur, Kishoreganj, Rajshahi, Tangail, Khulna and Sylhet.

The Dhaka region covers the Buriganga, the Balu River near Khilkhet, part of the Shitalakkhya, the Padma near Dohar and the Meghna near Narsingdi.

Regional data are available from January 2023 to September 2026. Over these three years and nine months, the highest number of bodies—398—were recovered in the Dhaka region, followed by Narayanganj with 253. Sylhet recorded the lowest number, at 20.

During the same period, 211 bodies were recovered in Barishal, 177 in Rajshahi, 167 in Chattogram, 149 in Faridpur, 127 each in Chandpur and Khulna, 94 in Kishoreganj and 93 in Tangail.

Dhaka also recorded the highest number of recoveries during the first nine months of this year, with 78 bodies. Barishal ranked second with 63, followed by Narayanganj with 60, Rajshahi with 55, Faridpur with 50, Tangail with 29, Khulna with 23, and Chattogram, Chandpur and Kishoreganj with 22 each. Six bodies were recovered in Sylhet.

Unidentified bodies hamper investigations

River police officials say many bodies have already begun decomposing before they surface. Fingerprints disappear and faces become disfigured, making identification difficult. Sometimes, only human skeletons are recovered.

Even when a post-mortem examination establishes evidence of murder, investigators may be unable to bring the perpetrators to justice if the victim's identity remains unknown. In other cases, the identity may eventually be established through various means, but decomposition makes it impossible to determine the cause of death.

Of the four bodies recovered from the Buriganga on 23 August, the body of a 30-year-old woman and that of a child aged three to four were found on the riverbank near the Mirerbag Cold Storage area in Keraniganj. The bodies of the young man and woman were recovered near Madaripur Ghat in Kalindi. All four bodies had begun decomposing. As no one came forward to claim them, Anjuman Mufidul Islam buried them as unidentified persons 11 days later.

Abdullah Al Mamun, superintendent of police for the Dhaka region of the River Police, told Prothom Alo that the killers had dumped the bodies in the river to conceal their crimes.

Two murder cases have been filed: one at South Keraniganj Police Station over the bodies of the woman and child, and another at Keraniganj Model Police Station over the bodies of the young man and woman. Photographs and DNA samples have been preserved. If anyone approaches the police stations looking for the missing individuals, investigators will attempt to establish their identities through DNA matching, he said.

Identity established through photographs and socks

On 16 January last year, river police recovered a man's body from the Shitalakkhya River in Narayanganj. The body was sent to the morgue at Narayanganj General Hospital for a post-mortem examination. The Kachpur River Police kept photographs of the body. As his identity could not be established, he was buried through Anjuman Mufidul Islam.

Later, his son Mahbubur Rahman identified the body as that of his father, Jabbar Hawlader, 45, by examining the photographs preserved by the police and the socks on the deceased man's feet. Jabbar worked as an autorickshaw driver. Mahbubur subsequently filed a murder case against unidentified individuals at Siddhirganj Police Station.

The investigation was assigned to Mainul Islam, a sub-inspector at the Kachpur River Police outpost. He is now serving at the River Police outpost under Bandar Police Station in Narayanganj.

Mainul Islam told Prothom Alo that the family had informed him that Jabbar had left home to drive his autorickshaw on 13 January last year and never returned. He had taken his mobile phone with him.

Following a lead from the phone, police detained a young man named Al Amin. During questioning, Al Amin said that a man named Shawon had sold him the phone.

Police subsequently detained and questioned Shawon. According to Mainul Islam, Shawon confessed to the murder and said that, after evening, he had lured Jabbar into consuming a soft drink mixed with an intoxicating substance and high-dose sleeping pills to render him unconscious, intending to steal his autorickshaw.

Jabbar was then removed from the autorickshaw while unconscious and thrown into the river from Adamjee Ghat in Narayanganj. Seven people shared the proceeds from the sale of the autorickshaw and the mobile phone, according to the account.

Mainul Islam said seven people involved in the crime had been arrested. Police recovered Jabbar's autorickshaw and mobile phone from them. Four of the accused gave confessional statements in court. They were members of an organised autorickshaw theft and robbery gang.

What post-mortem examinations reveal

River police sources say cases of unnatural death are generally filed when a body recovered from a river shows no signs of injury or has decomposed. However, if the condition of the body, physical evidence and surrounding circumstances suggest anything suspicious, river police file a murder case at the relevant police station, even if the victim's identity is unknown.

If an investigation and post-mortem examination establish that a death was a homicide, the case initially filed as an unnatural death is converted into a murder case, which the river police then investigate.

According to River Police Headquarters, post-mortem reports in confirmed homicide cases have cited rape, strangulation, head injuries and death caused by being thrown into water. River police have also recovered bodies with severed or injured hands, legs, necks and other body parts, as well as bodies wrapped in sacks. Murder cases are filed in such incidents.

Professor Mostaque Rahim, president of the Medicolegal Society of Bangladesh, told Prothom Alo that bodies recovered from rivers are often decomposed. Even when injuries or cuts are visible, decomposition can destroy crucial evidence. Fish and insects feeding on the bodies can also damage evidence, making it difficult to establish the cause of death.

In hot weather, bodies of people who have drowned may surface within 24 hours. If recovered at that stage, the cause of death can often be determined, he said.

Professor Mostaque Rahim added that the forensic medicine departments of government medical colleges in Bangladesh lacked modern equipment and laboratories. Establishing such facilities would help forensic experts assess deaths even when bodies had decomposed and determine the precise cause of death.

River police sources also said they collect general diaries (GDs) filed at police stations across the country concerning missing persons and investigate them with particular attention. Leads from these reports sometimes result in bodies being recovered from rivers.

Surveillance at river ghats and other potential dumping sites

Mohammad Rezaul Karim, additional inspector general of the River Police, told Prothom Alo that the circumstances surrounding a death cannot be unravelled if the victim's identity remains unknown.

Information obtained from investigations into murder cases involving bodies recovered from rivers indicates that killings are motivated by business disputes, family conflicts, disputes over drug trafficking, extramarital relationships and vehicle theft. After committing the murders, perpetrators dump the bodies in rivers to prevent identification, he said.

Asked why more bodies are recovered in the Dhaka and Narayanganj regions, the River Police chief said Dhaka, Narayanganj and Munshiganj are among the country's most densely populated areas. Business activity and employment opportunities are also concentrated there, and crime levels are correspondingly higher.

Asked what measures could prevent criminals from dumping bodies in rivers, Additional IGP Rezaul Karim said perpetrators often dispose of bodies in remote, isolated locations. The bodies subsequently drift with the current and are eventually recovered.

Police are analysing the waterways to identify the points used to dump bodies. Intelligence surveillance is being maintained around the clock at river ghats, riverside markets and roads. Several potential dumping sites, including Adamjee Ghat in Narayanganj, have been identified, and intelligence surveillance and patrols have been stepped up there, he said.

According to River Police data, Bangladesh has approximately 7,500 kilometres of navigable waterways during the monsoon, shrinking to around 4,500 kilometres in the dry season. Of this, approximately 3,500 kilometres are regularly used by watercraft. Ensuring security across this extensive network of waterways remains a major challenge for the River Police.

Professor Muhammad Umar Faruk of the Department of Criminology and Police Science at Mawlana Bhashani Science and Technology University in Tangail told Prothom Alo that professional criminals had come to regard waterways as safe places to dispose of bodies.

After rape and murder, perpetrators deliberately and carefully dump bodies into rivers from secluded locations to conceal their crimes. Such incidents are increasing, he said. Rivers have also been used to dispose of bodies following politically motivated killings at various times.

Professor Umar Faruk said criminals assume that even if a body surfaces, it will have decomposed and drifted from one place to another with the current. They believe the victim will remain unidentified and be buried as an unclaimed person.

To solve such cases, investigators must conduct thorough inquiries, gathering circumstantial evidence and applying psychological insight, he said. The criminologist recommended identifying potential dumping sites, increasing law enforcement surveillance and installing CCTV cameras to prevent bodies from being disposed of in rivers.
